research_question: Do independent Egyptian texts preserve a repeatable grammar in which damaged, removed, scattered, or contaminated parts of Horus are located, recovered, regrown, healed, or reintegrated by multiple divine agents?
admission_rule: A witness may support the Horus restoration grammar only when the text itself explicitly names Horus or an explicitly identified Horus-eye and an injury/loss plus at least one recovery/healing/regrowth action. Scholarly synthesis is stored separately from direct textual content.

primary_witnesses.source_type: Middle Kingdom Coffin Text 158 preserved/reworked as Book of the Dead 113
direct_text_support: Ra orders Sobek lord of the marsh to be brought to fish for/find the missing parts.
The text says Horus's mother made them grow in their place.
Sobek reports finding the place where the parts were scattered on the banks of the water and snaring them.
The text explicitly refers to discovery of the arms of Horus and a snare that brought the hands of Horus to him.
Ra gives Nekhen to Horus at the place of his arms/hands.
primary_witnesses.important_note: The UCL translation itself states that his mother made the missing parts grow in their place. This is stronger than the earlier registry wording that only described Sobek as a finder.

primary_witnesses.source_type: Papyrus Chester Beatty I, Contendings of Horus and Seth
primary_witnesses.translation_reference: Bibliotheca Alexandrina page cites M. Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature II, and W. K. Simpson, The Literature of Ancient Egypt.
direct_text_support: Seth removes Horus's two eyes from their sockets and buries them on the mountain.
The eyes become bulbs/lotuses in the narrative.
Hathor finds Horus, captures and milks a gazelle, and places the milk in the right and left eye.
Horus opens the eyes and Hathor verifies that they are healed.
Hathor reports that Seth deprived Horus of his eyes and that she restored him to health.

primary_witnesses.source_type: Coffin Text 335 / Book of the Dead 17
direct_text_support: The wedjat-eye is described as damaged on the day of the fight of Horus and Seth.
The explanatory gloss identifies injury to Horus in the fight.
Thoth is explicitly said to perform the restoration with his own fingers.
Another gloss describes Thoth treating the eye when it was ill/in tears.
A contextual explanatory layer calls the eye the right eye of Ra; this is a contextual gloss, not an exclusive identity rule.

primary_witnesses.source_type: Papyrus Chester Beatty I, Contendings of Horus and Seth
direct_text_support: Horus catches Seth's semen in his hands and shows it to Isis.
Isis uses a copper knife and cuts off Horus's hand(s).
The displayed Bibliotheca Alexandrina translation then proceeds to ointment and the semen-counterplot; it does not itself explicitly narrate a replacement hand in the immediately following passage.
primary_witnesses.relation_to_CT158: A scholarly synthesis by Gyula Priskin connects CT158 with this mythic hand episode and describes Isis as throwing the hands into water and growing new hands; JANUS does not silently promote that synthesis into wording absent from the displayed primary translation.

scholarly_synthesis.author: Gyula Priskin
scholarly_synthesis.work: The Ancient Egyptian Book of the Moon: Coffin Texts Spells 154-160
supports: CT 154-160 as an ordered lunar composition is an argued scholarly interpretation, not the only possible reading.
Priskin connects the hands of Horus in spell 158 with the Horus-Seth sexual-conflict hand episode and discusses severing, water, recovery by Sobek, and regrowth/replacement.

controls.supports: UCL summarizes the wider Osiris tradition in which Seth dismembers Osiris and Isis collects the limbs and revives the body sufficiently to conceive Horus.
controls.use: Positive control that Egyptian myth can explicitly encode collection/reconstitution of a divine body, while preventing transfer of Osiris-specific evidence to Horus.

controls.supports: The ritual includes explicit ordered actions and language about fastening a head to bones and purification.
controls.use: Procedure-language control; not a Horus body-restoration witness.

controls.supports: Body-part to deity mapping exists as an Egyptian textual grammar.
controls.use: Mapping control only; mapping is not injury, repair, or technology.
